newsitem.title: BOSNIA: U.S, NATO troops confiscate Bosnian army weapons.
newsitem.headline: U.S, NATO troops confiscate Bosnian army weapons.

text.p: U.S. troops confiscated hundreds of Kalashnikov assault rifles and tons of ammunition from a Bosnian army headquarters on Thursday in enforcement of the Dayton peace agreement, NATO said.

The American peacekeepers also towed away two Bosnian armoured personnel carriers, although Moslem civilians in the village of Celic tried to block the removal by forming a human barrier in the street.

NATO, which leads the Dayton peace implementation force, IFOR, has accused the Bosnian army's 254 Brigade of starting a violent incident in Gajevi, near Celic, on Tuesday, in which two people were reported to have been killed and a number of others wounded by gunfire.
The Moslems reacted furiously: "Somebody is blocking the Dayton peace agreement. For the moment it's IFOR," Avdo Hebib, Bosnian Interior Minister, told Reuters in Celic.
Brigadier-General Sead Delic, 2nd Bosnian Corps commander echoed his words: "This was a very imprudent act by IFOR."

NATO forces and U.N. police also raided a Bosnian Serb police station in Koraj, east of Gajevi, and confiscated seven automatic weapons, five rifle powered grenades and eight other weapons. NATO said Serb police had used the weapons to fire at Moslems in Gajevi on Tuesday.

NATO destroyed the arms by cutting each weapon into three pieces. It plans to ban all weapons in a 35 square km (13 square mile) "Temporary Restriction Zone" around Celic which it will begin enforcing on Saturday.

U.S. army General Montgomery Meigs, the new IFOR commander in the region, said IFOR was not restricting the refugees' freedom to return but instead was preventing distrust from blowing up into another war and eliminating threats to peace.

NATO spokesman Major Brett Boudreau said U.S. troops arrived unannounced at the 254 Brigade headquarters west of Celic at 5 a.m. on Thursday and removed several hundred Kalashnikovs and two five-tonne trucks of ammunition.
He said civilians had at one point blocked the passage of the Americans in an action which he described as "short-lived but serious and potentially threatening".
"Some rocks and stones were thrown at us and some of our personnel had to physically lift protesters off the road. Once they saw we were determined they made way," Boudreau said.
Thursday's operations at Celic and Koraj followed a decision by the international powers implementing the peace accord to suspend a refugee return process until the Gajevi crisis has been resolved.
